activity.overview: Compare how two poems about hope use form and figurative language to say different things.
activity.prompt: Emily Dickinson's "Hope" is the thing with feathers and "What Hope Sounds Like on a Tuesday" both use an extended metaphor for hope, but their forms are very different. Write an essay that compares the two poems. Explain each poem's extended metaphor and what it suggests about hope. Then compare their structures (stanzas, line length, rhyme and rhythm, punctuation) and analyze how each structure contributes to its meaning. Quote at least two lines from each poem.
activity.subject: english-language-arts
activity.title: Two Poems, Two Shapes

readings.attribution: Emily Dickinson (1830-1886). First published in Poems, Second Series (1891). Public domain.
readings.body:
"Hope" is the thing with feathers -
That perches in the soul -
And sings the tune without the words -
And never stops - at all -

And sweetest - in the Gale - is heard -
And sore must be the storm -
That could abash the little Bird
That kept so many warm -

I've heard it in the chillest land -
And on the strangest Sea -
Yet - never - in Extremity,
It asked a crumb - of Me.
readings.title: "Hope" is the thing with feathers

readings.body:
What Hope Sounds Like on a Tuesday

Not a bird.
Not anything with feathers.
More like the furnace in our basement
that clanks twice before it catches,
so that every winter morning
you lie there under three blankets
listening,
not sure,
and then
the long low breath of it
coming up through the floor.

Nobody writes songs about furnaces.
But my father taught me its sounds the way
other people learn birdsong:
the clank, the tick, the rush.
When it catches, he says,
you can stop waiting
and get up.
readings.title: What Hope Sounds Like on a Tuesday
